name: Hana Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and supervise the billing calls at a contact centre. I have a two-year college diploma, and people bring me the cases where a payment looks right until you check which household it belongs to. I’m good at this and earn more than most agents here. I do not use AI tools; I keep a paper list of the account numbers I need to inspect before I close a call.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Jules works at a hardware shop, and our two children are in school. We pay a mortgage and have around eight months of expenses set aside. There are many other centres in reach, though I dislike starting again with a new set of rules. I like putting a bill right while a customer is still speaking to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team AI Plateau sounds like another shortcut for routine bills. I would keep the manual account check before an agent tells someone the charge is settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead desk remains needed because small tools do not fix mixed-up households. Eight months saved and many centres nearby make the mortgage feel safe in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep supervising the billing calls and mark any repeat wrong-credit cases in our team book. In the first year of this mild change, I’d show two examples at the quality meeting so we keep enough time for a proper correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I prefer a slow correct answer to a quick apology that sends the customer back into the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake would you show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One customer’s payment was posted to a neighbour with the same surname. I found it from the account number, not the call summary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules (my partner) and I would leave the eight-month reserve alone. It is there for the mortgage and emergencies, not for a new gadget.

say: I’d insist on a **manual account check** for mixed-up bills.
I’d bring **wrong-credit examples** to the quality meeting.
think: I think my **lead desk** remains useful in this mild picture.
I trust **eight months saved** and nearby centres to protect the mortgage.
do: Keep **supervising billing calls** and log repeat wrong credits in 2026.
Show **two correction cases** at the first-year quality meeting.
S0.quote: I prefer a slow correct answer to a quick apology that sends the customer back into the queue.
fieldNote: She trusts **account numbers** over a generated call summary.
The **eight-month reserve** already exists; she does not add a new saving plan.
Her quality meeting is a **technical presentation**, not a shared worker demand.

steps.text: Keep supervising billing calls and log repeat wrong-credit cases

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption could answer the easy bills and leave us with the ones that require a person to untangle two accounts. I would ask management for the paid hours behind its new plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my careful work still matters, but there may be fewer lead shifts. Jules earns a wage too and we have savings, so I can compare local centres rather than jump at the first title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep a ledger of reopened billing errors and ask my manager for the paid lead rota. In the first year routine chats move, I’d apply for a posted paid billing job at another centre only if its written weekly wage and hours cover the mortgage after travel and fit our children’s pickup; I’d stay put until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the rota. I can handle a new workplace, but I do not want a job that pays well only on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the ledger count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count the cases that come back because a credit went to the wrong account. A chat count alone hides that extra work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which shift would you reject?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules (my partner) closes the hardware shop on some evenings. I would check the new centre’s late shifts before agreeing to leave our current routine.

say: I’d ask for the **paid lead rota** behind management’s plan.
I’d show **reopened billing errors** rather than closed-chat totals.
think: I think my **careful billing work** remains needed.
I fear **fewer lead shifts**, despite wages and savings at home.
do: Log **reopened billing errors** and ask for paid lead hours in 2026.
Apply for **posted paid billing work** only with written after-travel mortgage-covering wages/hours and pickup; stay until a signed offer.
S1.quote: I can handle a new workplace, but I do not want a job that pays well only on paper.
fieldNote: She makes an **individual manager inquiry**, not a collective demand.
She has **nearby alternatives** and eight months of savings.
A job move requires **whole-week net pay** and school pickup.

steps.text: Keep logging reopened billing errors and ask for paid lead hours
Apply for posted billing with written after-travel mortgage-covering wages/hours fitting pickup and Jules’s evening rota
Keep current shift until a suitable billing offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 could make the billing judgement and speak to the customer. Robots around 2031 arrive later, but a desk worker does not get those extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead shifts might end despite the care I put into them. Eight months saved gives us time, but a mortgage cannot be paid forever from a reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask for the written date of any staff cut and compare posted paid reception roles at nearby offices. If my hours end in the first year after 2028, I’d move only where a signed offer gives written weekly wages and hours covering the mortgage after travel and any extra childcare; I would keep my current shift until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and slower to trust a new role than a new label. Eight months is a cushion, not a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you inspect in reception?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask what the receptionist can actually change in a visitor’s account. If the job is only reading a screen, AGI will reach it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the children be picked up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules (my partner) and I would set our work rotas beside the children’s school hours. A paid after-school place is possible, but its cost has to fit the new wage.

say: I’d demand **written cut dates** for paid billing shifts before I compare other jobs.
I’d say **2028 AGI** reaches our desk before robots.
think: I think my **lead shifts** could end despite my skill.
I know **eight months saved** cannot replace wages indefinitely.
do: Request **written staff-cut dates** and inspect posted reception jobs in 2026.
Move after hours end only to **posted paid reception** on signed written mortgage-covering weekly wages/hours after travel/childcare, with workable school care.
feel: **Anxious** about a wage gap, with search time.
S2.quote: Eight months saved gives us time, but a mortgage cannot be paid forever from a reserve.
fieldNote: Her **reserve buys time** to compare several local offices.
She questions whether a **reception job** has work AGI cannot also do.
Any offer must cover **extra childcare** after travel costs.

steps.text: Inspect posted paid reception openings at nearby offices before 2028
Move after hours end to posted reception on signed written net mortgage-covering wages/hours and school care

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives me time to look at real office work while I keep my billing wage. I would ask a nearby housing office whether its paid account-correction job is actually posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could use my payment skill there, but full thinking AI may also match transactions in 2031. I do not want to pay for training without a wage attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask for a supervised paid trial in housing accounts only if the office posts a paid opening. If its posted role requires a records course, I’d take it only when the employer pays the fee and my study hours. In the first year after 2031, I’d move only on a signed offer with written weekly pay and hours covering our mortgage after travel and childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, though five years gives me room to inspect the ledger. A course certificate is not a pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the paid trial involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would follow one tenant credit from the payment to the corrected account during a paid shift. If I cannot actually change a wrong entry, the role is not an improvement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Jules assess the rota?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules (my partner) would check whether the office closes before school pickup. I would not accept a longer trip simply because the job title sounds safer.

say: I’d ask whether **paid housing-account work** is actually posted.
I’d ask for a **supervised paid trial** tied to a posted opening.
think: I think my **payment skill** could transfer to housing accounts.
I know **2031 AGI** could match transactions there too.
do: Seek **supervised paid housing trial** only for a posted paid opening in 2026.
Take **required funded records course** only on paid study hours for that vacancy.
Move after 2031 only with **signed written weekly wages/hours** covering mortgage after travel/childcare, account-correction authority and workable pickup.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to inspect the ledger.
S3.quote: A course certificate is not a pay packet.
fieldNote: The **trial is paid** and conditional on a posted job.
A required course needs **employer-paid fees and hours**.
The move needs **account authority**, net pay and school-compatible travel.

steps.text: Try supervised paid housing-accounts shift only for a posted paid opening
Take role-required records course only with employer-paid fees and study hours
Move only on signed written net mortgage-covering weekly wages/hours with correction authority and workable school pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us years to see whether a local employer still pays people to fix accounts. I would check actual vacancies each spring rather than guess at a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can keep the higher wage for some years and protect our eight-month reserve. Full thinking AI might still do billing decisions in 2036, with hands-on robots coming around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading billing calls and make a yearly list of posted account jobs within our school journey. In the first year after 2036, if my paid hours fall, I’d move only to a posted job on a signed offer showing weekly wages and hours covering the mortgage after travel and childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later end, settled enough for this year. I can watch a decade of rotas without quitting a good wage today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your yearly list include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the whole paid week at each office, not just the hourly rate. A job can have a higher rate and fewer shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the family relocate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules (my partner) and I would keep our children at their school unless a signed offer paid the mortgage after a different home and commute. With so many local jobs, we need not move the family for a rumour.

say: I’d check **posted account jobs** each spring.
I’d compare **whole-week wages** rather than job titles or hourly rates.
think: I think my **higher wage** may last several years.
I know **2036 thinking AI** could still take billing decisions.
do: Keep **leading billing calls** and list posted local account jobs yearly.
Move after hours fall only to **posted paid work** on signed written weekly wages/hours covering mortgage after travel and childcare.
Consider **moving home** only with signed pay covering the mortgage after housing and commute.
S4.quote: I can watch a decade of rotas without quitting a good wage today.
fieldNote: Her **eight-month reserve** stays intact without a new savings pledge.
She checks **posted jobs yearly** rather than assuming a future opening.
The family move needs **net mortgage-covering pay** and a signed offer.

steps.text: Keep leading paid billing calls while hours remain
Move after hours fall to posted accounts only on signed written net mortgage-covering weekly wages/hours
Consider moving home only with signed offer covering mortgage after housing and commute
List posted local account jobs and compare full paid weeks each spring

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. If thinking AI takes billing decisions as well as calls, my skill may be cheap to copy, though eight months saved gives us time to check nearby employers. Written cut dates and a posted paid role with reliable whole-week pay would help; I would not leave my current wage for an unsigned promise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I would ask who pays for a wrong credit when software closes the case. The customer should not have to prove the same wrong credit to a fourth agent.

headlineQuote: The customer should not have to prove the same wrong credit to a fourth agent.
portrait: At **43**, Hana supervises difficult billing calls with a two-year diploma and higher pay.
She and Jules support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with about eight months of expenses saved.
She **never uses AI** and checks account numbers herself before closing a call.
She weighs **posted local work** carefully and avoids changing jobs on an unsigned promise.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could copy her billing decisions before a safe job move is ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut dates** and a posted role with reliable mortgage-covering weekly pay would help.
